title: IPMAT Indore VA Sectional – 7th Nov 2026 (Advanced Analytical)

passages.RC1:
Proposals to tax the very rich have returned to politics in many countries. In France a plan for a minimum annual tax on the largest fortunes has been debated with unusual heat; in Brazil and elsewhere, governments have raised the idea in international forums; and in India the concentration of wealth at the top has been the subject of studies that attract both citation and dispute. The argument for such taxes is easily stated. Fortunes at the top have grown faster than incomes, and because the wealthy consume only a small part of what they own, much of their wealth escapes the taxes that fall on spending and wages. A levy on the stock of wealth would, its supporters say, restore a measure of fairness and raise revenue from those most able to pay.

The objections are mainly practical, and they are not trivial. Wealth is harder to measure than income. A salary appears on a payslip, but the value of a private company, a collection of art or a stake in a start-up can be known only by estimate, and estimates invite dispute and avoidance. A further problem is timing: since the tax would be levied annually, a fall in asset prices could leave an owner paying tax on gains that had already vanished. Several European countries that introduced wealth taxes in the twentieth century later repealed them, having found that the revenue was small, the administrative costs high and the exodus of wealthy residents costly. Critics conclude that wealth taxes fail not through any flaw in their aims but because the thing taxed is mobile, illiquid and difficult to value.

Defenders reply that the lessons of past failures are specific and avoidable. The old taxes had many exemptions, which invited the rich to rearrange their assets into the exempt categories, and low thresholds that hit the merely well-off while leaving the very rich unaffected. A modern tax, they argue, could have a very high threshold, a broad base with few exemptions, and rules that make departure costly, such as an exit tax on those who leave. International cooperation would help, since wealth moves easily across borders, and automatic exchange of information between tax authorities has already reduced the scope for hiding assets. Whether such a design can be enforced against owners with the means to hire the best advice is, however, the central empirical question, and the evidence is thin because few such taxes have been tried.

A subtler difficulty concerns liquidity. The founder of a company may be worth billions on paper while holding little cash; his wealth consists of shares in a firm that pays no dividend. A tax of two per cent a year would require him to sell shares, which could weaken his control and, for a young firm, reduce its capacity to invest. Supporters propose allowing payment in kind or deferral, but these devices complicate the tax and reduce its yield. There is also a question of principle. A tax on wealth falls on assets that have already been taxed when the income that created them was earned, so that it may be seen as double taxation; defenders reply that wealth, in the form of unrealised gains, has often escaped income tax altogether, and that a wealth tax is a substitute for the tax that was never paid.

The debate is often conducted as though the choice were between a wealth tax and nothing. The alternatives deserve attention: higher taxes on capital gains and inheritances, closing the loopholes that allow gains to be passed on untaxed at death, and minimum taxes on the income of the very rich. These are less dramatic but easier to administer, because they tax events that can be observed, such as a sale or a bequest, and not a stock that must be valued. Their weakness is that they permit the deferral of tax for as long as the asset is held. The sensible course may be to judge each proposal by two tests: whether it can be administered against those it aims at, and whether its revenue and fairness gains justify its costs in lost investment and effort. A tax that fails the first test cannot pass the second.
passages.RC2:
Few questions in Indian education arouse as much feeling as the language in which children are taught. The stakes are large, for the language of instruction shapes who learns, how much, and with what prospects. The National Education Policy encourages instruction in the mother tongue or a regional language at least until the fifth grade, and states have long argued over how many languages students must learn and in what order. Supporters of mother-tongue instruction point to the evidence that children learn to read most easily in a language they speak and understand. Opponents point to the labour market, where English is the language of higher education, of much of the private sector and of social mobility. Both are right, and the difficulty lies in the fact that their truths pull in different directions.

The pedagogical evidence is reasonably clear. A child who is taught in an unfamiliar language must decode the language and the content at once, and is therefore likely to learn less of both. Studies in many countries find that children who begin in the mother tongue and add a second language gradually do better in reading and in other subjects than those who are placed in a second-language classroom from the start. Some evidence also suggests that skills learnt in the first language transfer to the second, so that time spent on the mother tongue is not time lost. The argument is not against learning English but against using English to teach a child who does not yet understand it.

The economic evidence points in a different direction, or appears to. English proficiency is associated with higher wages in India, and surveys suggest that parents, including poor parents, are willing to pay for English-medium private schools even where the quality of instruction is poor. The returns to English may, moreover, reflect other advantages that go with it, such as urban residence and family income, so that the wage premium overstates what English alone would deliver. The parents' preference is rational given the returns they observe, but it generates a problem of its own: schools that teach in English to children who do not speak it at home may deliver neither the language nor the learning, leaving pupils with weak skills in both. A policy that ignores the parents' wishes risks being ignored in turn, as families move their children to schools that give them what they want.

The apparent conflict can be reduced by distinguishing medium from subject. A school may teach in the mother tongue while teaching English well as a subject, and well-designed programmes do this. The difficulty is not in the principle but in the resources it requires. Textbooks and trained teachers are needed in many languages, including those with few speakers; a country with hundreds of languages must decide which to support, and the decision is political. In a state with several major languages, the choice of the regional language may disadvantage minorities, and children of migrant workers, who move between states, may find themselves in classrooms where the medium changes with the border. These costs are not decisive arguments against the policy, but they explain why implementation lags behind aspiration.

The politics of language add a further layer. Language is an emblem of identity, and a policy that appears to favour one language over another is read as a statement about who belongs. The proposal that students should learn three languages has been welcomed in some states and resisted in others, which see it as a vehicle for the promotion of a national language at the expense of regional ones. It would be a mistake to treat these objections as mere politics: they express a concern that the state's educational authority should not be used to dilute the languages of its citizens. The experience of countries that have changed the medium of instruction, sometimes more than once, suggests that continuity matters, since each change disrupts a generation of learners. A policy that rests on the evidence about learning, offers real access to English, and respects the languages of the regions is more likely to succeed than one that is imposed from above or left to the market.
passages.RC3:
Most of what is secret on the internet, from bank transfers to private messages, relies on mathematical problems that are easy to pose and extremely hard to solve. Factoring a very large number into its prime components, for example, would take a conventional computer longer than the age of the universe, and the difficulty protects the keys on which encryption depends. Quantum computers, which exploit the behaviour of matter at very small scales, are expected to solve some such problems exponentially faster. An algorithm devised in the 1990s showed that a sufficiently large quantum machine could break the most widely used public-key systems. The consequences would extend beyond privacy, since the same techniques secure software updates and digital signatures, on which trust in electronic commerce depends. No such machine exists today, but the possibility has been enough to make governments and companies begin to prepare.

The central uncertainty is when. Estimates of the arrival of a machine capable of breaking current encryption range from a decade to several, and experts differ as to whether the engineering difficulties, above all the correction of the errors to which quantum bits are prone, will yield to steady progress or require breakthroughs. Under such uncertainty it is tempting to wait. The temptation is dangerous because of a feature that distinguishes this problem from most security risks: an adversary can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it later, when the machine is available. This is called harvest now, decrypt later, and it means that information with a long shelf life, such as state secrets, medical records and industrial designs, is already at risk even though the threat has not materialised. Even a modest chance of such a machine within the lifetime of the data it could expose is enough to justify precaution.

The remedy is post-quantum cryptography, a family of algorithms based on problems that are believed to resist quantum attack. Standards bodies have selected candidate algorithms after years of public scrutiny, and governments have set dates by which sensitive systems must migrate. But migration is neither quick nor cheap. Encryption is embedded in devices, protocols and software that were built decades ago and are rarely documented; many organisations do not know where it is used. The change must be made across banks, telecom networks, power grids and millions of devices, some of which, such as chips in vehicles and meters, cannot easily be updated. The scale resembles that of the effort to deal with the year-2000 bug, with the difference that the deadline is unknown. Smaller organisations, which lack specialist staff, will depend on their suppliers to make the change on their behalf, and an inventory of where encryption is used is the first step.

There is also a question of trust in the new algorithms themselves. The older systems have survived decades of attack by skilled cryptographers; the new ones have had far less. History offers cases in which schemes thought secure were broken by a clever idea, and some candidates have fallen during the selection process. A premature migration to an algorithm that is later found to be weak would be worse than no migration. Many experts therefore recommend a hybrid approach, in which data are protected by both a classical and a post-quantum algorithm, so that an attacker must break both. The cost is greater complexity and some loss of speed, but it provides insurance against the failure of either.

The episode illustrates a general problem in managing technological risk: the tension between acting early under uncertainty and acting late at greater cost. Those who warn early are often accused of alarmism if the danger fails to arrive, and those who delay may be blamed if it comes. A rational policy weighs the cost of preparation against the probability and severity of the harm and its irreversibility. For quantum threats, the factors favour early action for long-lived data, because the harm cannot be undone once the data have been taken, but not for short-lived data, which lose their value before any machine is likely to exist. India, with a large digital financial system and an ambitious national quantum mission, has an interest in both the technology and its defence.
passages.CA1:
CONVERSATION ANALYSIS: Read the following transcript and choose the answer that is closest to each of the questions that are based on the transcript.

Tanvi Rao (Host, Everyday Economics): Every festival season, flight and train fares jump. Is that just greed?

Dr. Karan Mehta (economist): It looks like greed, but it is mostly scarcity. A plane has a fixed number of seats, and when many more people want to travel on the same few days, either the price rises until demand matches supply, or the seats go to whoever books first. A fare that rises with demand rations the seats to those who value them most, and it also signals the airline to add flights.

Tanvi Rao: But that seems unfair to those who cannot plan ahead.

Dr. Karan Mehta: Fairness is the real objection, and it is a fair one. People accept high prices when they believe costs have risen, as with a hotel at a premium during a conference. They resent them when the only change is demand. The result is that firms hide dynamic prices in complicated fare classes, which makes the system harder to understand and invites suspicion.

Tanvi Rao: So should regulators cap fares?

Dr. Karan Mehta: Caps lower the price but not the scarcity. Seats then go to the fastest clickers or to touts, and the airline has less reason to add flights. A cap is a way of saying that a high price is unacceptable without doing anything about the shortage that caused it.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: Wealth taxes raise real administrative problems, so each proposal should be judged on enforceability and net benefit
Wealth taxes have failed everywhere they have been tried, and governments should therefore abandon every proposal to tax wealth
Wealth taxes are unnecessary, since the very rich already pay more in taxes on their spending than they do in taxes on their wealth
Wealth taxes are the only fair way of taxing the very rich, and the objections to them have all been answered by their supporters
questions.explanation: The author sets out the case, the objections and the replies, and concludes that each proposal be judged by 'whether it can be administered against those it aims at' and whether its gains justify its costs. The other options adopt one side.

questions.question: According to the passage, several European countries repealed their wealth taxes because
options: the voters of those countries had decided that the rich should not be taxed on the value of their possessions
courts had ruled that a tax on wealth was a form of double taxation which the laws of those countries forbade
the rich in those countries had agreed to pay higher taxes on their incomes in place of a tax on wealth
the revenue was small, the costs of administration high and the departure of wealthy residents costly
questions.explanation: The passage says the countries repealed them 'having found that the revenue was small, the administrative costs high and the exodus of wealthy residents costly'.

questions.question: Defenders say the failures of past wealth taxes were avoidable because they
options: were caused by the unwillingness of the wealthy to disclose the value of their assets to the tax authorities
were due to exemptions and low thresholds, which a modern design could avoid
arose from the fact that international cooperation between tax authorities did not exist in any form
showed that taxes on wealth cannot raise more revenue than taxes on income of the same kind
questions.explanation: The passage says the old taxes had 'many exemptions' and 'low thresholds', and that a modern tax 'could have a very high threshold, a broad base with few exemptions, and rules that make departure costly'.

questions.question: The author uses the example of a company founder to show that
options: wealth may be large on paper while cash is scarce, forcing a sale of shares
founders of companies are more likely than other wealthy people to move their assets abroad
wealth consisting of shares can be valued more easily than wealth consisting of works of art
a tax of two per cent a year would be too low to raise any significant revenue from founders
questions.explanation: The passage says the founder 'may be worth billions on paper while holding little cash', so a tax 'would require him to sell shares, which could weaken his control'.

questions.question: The defenders' reply to the charge of double taxation is that
options: income tax is a more efficient way of taxing the rich than a tax on the value of their wealth
the rich are able to pay both taxes, since their wealth grows faster than the rate at which it is taxed
unrealised gains have often escaped income tax, so the wealth tax replaces a tax never paid
wealth is always created from income that has already been taxed, and it should not be taxed a second time
questions.explanation: The passage says 'wealth, in the form of unrealised gains, has often escaped income tax altogether, and that a wealth tax is a substitute for the tax that was never paid'.

questions.question: Each of the following is mentioned as an alternative to a wealth tax EXCEPT
options: closing the loopholes that let gains pass untaxed at death
minimum taxes on the income of the very rich
higher taxes on capital gains and inheritances
abolishing inheritance taxes to encourage saving
questions.explanation: The last paragraph lists the first three. The abolition of inheritance taxes is never suggested.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: The three-language policy has failed, since it has been resisted by states that regard it as a threat to their regional languages
Mother-tongue instruction should be adopted in every school, since parents have no right to choose the language of their children
English should be the medium of instruction from the first grade, since it is the language of higher education and of the private sector
The evidence favours mother-tongue instruction, but resources, labour-market returns and identity politics complicate its adoption
questions.explanation: The author presents the learning evidence, the economic evidence, the resource costs and the politics, and concludes that a policy resting on evidence, giving access to English and respecting regional languages is likelier to succeed. The other options adopt one side.

questions.question: According to the passage, a child taught in an unfamiliar language is likely to learn less because
options: textbooks in unfamiliar languages contain fewer examples drawn from the daily lives of the children
teachers who use an unfamiliar language are less well trained than teachers who use the mother tongue
the child must decode the language and the content at once
children who are taught in an unfamiliar language are less willing to attend school regularly
questions.explanation: The passage says 'A child who is taught in an unfamiliar language must decode the language and the content at once, and is therefore likely to learn less of both'.

questions.question: The author says that parents' preference for English-medium schools is rational but that it
options: should be ignored by policy-makers, since parents are not qualified to judge the value of a language
can produce schools that deliver neither the language nor the learning
proves that English is more useful than any regional language in the labour market of every state
shows that poor parents value education less than parents who can afford the fees of better schools
questions.explanation: The passage says the preference 'is rational given the returns they observe, but it generates a problem of its own: schools that teach in English to children who do not speak it at home may deliver neither the language nor the learning'.

questions.question: The distinction between medium and subject is meant to show that
options: a school may teach in the mother tongue while teaching English well as a subject
the medium of instruction matters less than the number of languages that students are required to learn
English should be dropped as a subject in schools that teach in the mother tongue of the children
a school which teaches English as a subject cannot use the mother tongue as its medium of instruction
questions.explanation: The passage says 'A school may teach in the mother tongue while teaching English well as a subject, and well-designed programmes do this'.

questions.question: Each of the following is mentioned as a cost of implementing mother-tongue instruction EXCEPT that
options: textbooks and trained teachers are needed in many languages
it lowers children's reading scores in the first years of school
children of migrant workers may meet a change of medium at the border
the choice of a regional language may disadvantage minorities
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph mentions the first three costs. The passage says mother-tongue instruction helps reading, so it does not lower scores.

questions.question: According to the passage, some states resist the three-language proposal because they
options: believe that children cannot learn three languages without a decline in their ability in each of them
wish to teach only English in schools, since it is the language of the labour market
are unable to find enough teachers who can teach all three languages in their schools
see it as a vehicle for promoting a national language at the expense of regional ones
questions.explanation: The passage says it is resisted in states 'which see it as a vehicle for the promotion of a national language at the expense of regional ones'.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: Quantum computing threatens encryption, and early migration is prudent for long-lived data
Quantum computers able to break encryption already exist, and all digital communication should be regarded as insecure
Post-quantum algorithms have been proved secure, and organisations should migrate to them as quickly as they possibly can
The threat from quantum computers is exaggerated, and governments should wait until a working machine has been built
questions.explanation: The author explains the threat, the uncertainty about timing, harvest-now-decrypt-later, the difficulty of migration and the case for early action on long-lived data. The other options contradict this.

questions.question: 'Harvest now, decrypt later' means that
options: an adversary can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it when a quantum machine is available
quantum computers will be able to decrypt messages only if they are sent after the machines are built
encryption keys are collected by governments and held in secret until quantum computers are built
encrypted data are destroyed after a period of time, and so cannot be decrypted by later machines
questions.explanation: The passage says 'an adversary can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it later, when the machine is available'.

questions.question: According to the passage, migration to post-quantum cryptography is difficult because
options: governments have forbidden private organisations to change the encryption that they now use
encryption is embedded in undocumented devices and software, some not updatable
post-quantum algorithms are too slow to be used for any purpose in banks or telecom networks
standards bodies have not yet agreed on any algorithm that could be used for the purpose
questions.explanation: The passage says encryption is 'embedded in devices, protocols and software that were built decades ago and are rarely documented' and that some devices 'cannot easily be updated'.

questions.question: A hybrid approach protects data by
options: replacing the classical algorithm with a post-quantum algorithm once the latter has been tested
encrypting data twice with the same algorithm, so that an attacker must break it two times
using a classical and a post-quantum algorithm together, so an attacker must break both
using a quantum computer to protect the data against attacks by other quantum computers
questions.explanation: The passage says data are protected 'by both a classical and a post-quantum algorithm, so that an attacker must break both'.

questions.question: The comparison with the year-2000 bug suggests that the effort needed is
options: similar in scale, but the deadline for the quantum threat is unknown
smaller in scale, since quantum threats affect fewer systems than the year-2000 bug did
unnecessary, since the year-2000 bug proved to have been much exaggerated by experts
identical in every respect, including the date by which the work must be completed
questions.explanation: The passage says 'The scale resembles that of the effort to deal with the year-2000 bug, with the difference that the deadline is unknown'.

questions.question: The author's view is that early action is justified for
options: no data, since the cost of preparation is greater than the probability of any harm
long-lived data, since the harm cannot be undone once they have been taken
short-lived data, since they are the most likely to be taken by an adversary
all data, since any information may be recorded by an adversary and used later
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the factors favour early action 'for long-lived data, because the harm cannot be undone once the data have been taken, but not for short-lived data'.

questions.question: According to Dr. Mehta, fares rise in the festival season mainly because
options: seats are fixed and demand surges, so price rations seats and signals airlines to add flights
airlines wish to raise their profits and take advantage of passengers who cannot travel on other days
the cost of operating a flight rises sharply in the festival season, since fuel and staff cost more
regulators allow airlines to set fares without any limit on the amount that they can charge
questions.explanation: She says 'It looks like greed, but it is mostly scarcity', and that a fare that rises with demand 'rations the seats to those who value them most, and it also signals the airline to add flights'.

questions.question: Dr. Mehta says people resent dynamic prices when
options: the airline adds flights in order to meet the demand that is caused by the festival season
regulators have capped the fares of the airlines that fly on the busiest routes in the country
the prices are shown in complicated fare classes that they are unable to understand fully
the only change is demand, though they accept prices when costs have risen
questions.explanation: She says 'People accept high prices when they believe costs have risen... They resent them when the only change is demand'.

questions.question: Dr. Mehta's objection to fare caps is that they
options: are unfair to airlines, which must meet the cost of operating the flights from the revenue they earn
raise the price of tickets for the passengers who book in advance, and so harm those who plan ahead
force airlines to add flights even when they cannot do so without making a loss on those flights
lower the price but not the scarcity, so seats go to the fastest clickers or touts
questions.explanation: She says 'Caps lower the price but not the scarcity. Seats then go to the fastest clickers or to touts, and the airline has less reason to add flights'.

questions.question: The politician's ________ answer, a thicket of qualifications, allowed him to claim after the debate that he had been misunderstood.
options: forthright
unequivocal
transparent
evasive
questions.explanation: 'Evasive' means avoiding a direct answer, which a thicket of qualifications allows. 'Unequivocal', 'transparent' and 'forthright' are direct, and would not permit a claim of being misunderstood.

questions.question: The firm's ________ growth, which owed more to acquisitions than to sales, impressed analysts less than the headline figures suggested.
options: exponential
inorganic
sustainable
spontaneous
questions.explanation: 'Inorganic' growth comes from buying other firms rather than from the firm's own sales. 'Spontaneous', 'sustainable' and 'exponential' do not describe growth that owes more to acquisitions.

questions.question: With sales falling, the company decided to ________ and reduce every department's budget by a tenth.
options: cry over spilt milk
rest on its oars
blow its own trumpet
tighten its belt
questions.explanation: 'Tighten its belt' means to economise. 'Rest on its oars' is to relax after effort, 'blow its own trumpet' is to boast, and 'cry over spilt milk' is to lament what cannot be undone.

questions.question: Though the judge's manner was ________, his rulings were fair and, on close reading, remarkably lenient.
options: indulgent
austere
effusive
genial
questions.explanation: 'Though' sets up a contrast: an 'austere' (stern) manner against lenient rulings. 'Genial', 'effusive' and 'indulgent' would not contrast with leniency.

questions.question: The ________ of the regulator, which had ________ the warnings for years, was exposed when the collapse revealed how little it had ________ the risks.
options: complacency; ignored; disregarded
complacency; heeded; grasped
complacency; ignored; grasped
vigilance; ignored; grasped
questions.explanation: A regulator that ignored warnings and had not grasped the risks showed 'complacency'. 'Vigilance' and 'heeded' contradict the failure; 'how little it had disregarded the risks' is illogical.

questions.question: A ________ student, he mastered every subject, and yet he lacked the ________ to apply what he knew to a new problem.
options: diligent; ingenuity
diligent; honesty
idle; ingenuity
diligent; indifference
questions.explanation: A 'diligent' student who mastered every subject but lacked the 'ingenuity' (inventiveness) to apply it. 'Idle' contradicts mastering every subject; 'honesty' and 'indifference' do not suit applying knowledge to a new problem.

questions.question: The agreement was less a settlement than a ________: it postponed the quarrel without resolving any of the questions that caused it.
options: resolution
truce
reconciliation
verdict
questions.explanation: A 'truce' is a pause in conflict without resolution. 'Verdict', 'reconciliation' and 'resolution' imply that the quarrel was settled.

questions.question: Her ________ prose, with its long sentences and dense qualifications, demanded patience that few readers could spare.
options: unadorned
lucid
tortuous
crisp
questions.explanation: 'Tortuous' means twisting and complicated, matching long sentences and dense qualifications. 'Crisp', 'lucid' and 'unadorned' describe clear, plain prose.

questions.question: His ________ was such that he could be relied upon to say what he thought, whatever the consequences to himself.
options: candour
diffidence
duplicity
subterfuge
questions.explanation: 'Candour' means frankness, fitting someone who says what he thinks whatever the cost. 'Duplicity' and 'subterfuge' mean deceit; 'diffidence' means shyness.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The ambassador was recalled after his remarks caused considerable embarrassment to his government at home.
A thin layer of frost covered the fields when the farmers rose at dawn to begin the harvest of the crop.
The firm continued to flaunt the safety regulations, ignoring repeated warnings.
The architect's design was widely admired for its elegant proportions and economy of means in every respect.
questions.explanation: To disregard a rule openly is to 'flout' it; 'flaunt' means to show off. 'Elegant', 'frost' and 'recalled' are used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The two firms entered into a partnership that proved beneficial to both of them within the first year of work.
It was a torturous route through the hills, winding back on itself at every turn.
Her testimony was corroborated by two independent witnesses who had been present at the scene of the accident.
The treaty was negotiated in secret and ratified by the legislature without any public discussion of its terms.
questions.explanation: A winding route is 'tortuous'; 'torturous' means causing torture. 'Ratified', 'corroborated' (confirmed) and 'beneficial' are used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The old library, though cramped, contained a collection of rare manuscripts of great value to scholars.
He gave a lucid account of the events, which the jury found easy to follow in every respect and detail.
She ordered a supply of stationary for the office: pens, paper and envelopes.
The train remained stationary for an hour while engineers repaired a fault on the line ahead of it.
questions.explanation: Pens, paper and envelopes are 'stationery'; 'stationary' means not moving. 'Stationary' in the second sentence, 'lucid' and 'manuscripts' are correct.

questions.question: He insisted <u>to pay</u> the bill.
options: to be paying
for paying
in paying
on paying
questions.explanation: 'Insist' takes 'on' followed by a gerund: 'insisted on paying'.

questions.question: If it <u>will rain</u> tomorrow, the match will be cancelled.
options: rains
rained
would rain
is raining
questions.explanation: In a first conditional the 'if' clause takes the present simple, not 'will': 'If it rains tomorrow'.

questions.question: The books <u>that was</u> lost have been found.
options: who were
which was being
that were
that has been
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun 'that' refers to the plural 'books', so the verb is plural: 'that were lost'.

questions.question: She <u>cannot hardly</u> hear the speaker.
options: cannot barely
can hardly
could not hardly
can't hardly
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' already has a negative sense, so it is not used with 'not': 'can hardly hear'.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

Scientific consensus is sometimes treated as a vote. ____________________. It is better understood as the convergence of independent lines of evidence: when physicists, chemists and geologists using different methods arrive at the same age for the Earth, agreement reflects the strength of the evidence and not the popularity of a view.
options: Agreement among scientists is rare, and no conclusion has ever been accepted by the whole of the scientific community.
Consensus is reached when the most senior scientists in a field announce which conclusion all others must accept.
Scientists decide what is true by holding elections in which the majority view is declared to be the conclusion.
It is not a vote, since conclusions gain weight from evidence and not from numbers.
questions.explanation: The next sentences explain consensus as convergence of evidence, so the blank must reject the idea of a vote. The other options contradict this.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

Monuments to the dead of war seem to speak with one voice. ____________________. The names inscribed on them rarely say who chose to fight and who was conscripted, nor what was thought of the war by those who died; the stone records the loss and passes over the dispute.
options: Most war memorials were erected by governments that wished to conceal the number of soldiers who had died in battle.
Those who died in wars are remembered more fully by the memorials than by the histories that have been written.
Yet they say less than they appear to, since they record loss and omit contested meaning.
Memorials are always accurate records of the courage and character of each person whose name is inscribed upon them.
questions.explanation: 'Seem' and the following sentences show that memorials omit contested meaning, so the blank begins 'Yet they say less'. The other options contradict this.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

Early railways were built by private companies in competition. ____________________. Different gauges, signals and timetables made through travel difficult, and it took regulation, and in some countries nationalisation, to make the separate lines into a network.
options: The companies that built railways competed on price, and so fares were lower than they have been since.
Nationalisation has always produced a better railway than competition between private companies could have achieved.
Competition produced lines, but a network required coordination that competition did not supply.
Railways were built successfully by private companies alone, and no regulation was needed to create a network.
questions.explanation: The next sentence says regulation or nationalisation was needed to create a network, so the blank states that competition did not supply coordination. The other options contradict this.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. It explains why rising incomes have not always made societies happier.
2. Psychologists call this the hedonic treadmill: people adapt to improvements and want more.
3. A raise or a new house brings a burst of satisfaction.
4. Yet within months, most return to roughly their earlier level of happiness.
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 gives the first effect. Sentence 4 ('Yet') gives the reversal. Sentence 2 ('this') names it. Sentence 1 ('It explains') draws the implication. Order: 3-4-2-1.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. Whether subsidies can reproduce the advantages of scale and experience remains uncertain.
2. Such concentration, however, creates a risk for every country that depends on the chips.
3. A single firm in Taiwan makes most of the world's most advanced chips.
4. Governments elsewhere, anxious about dependence, have begun to subsidise plants at home.
5. The reason is that fabrication has enormous fixed costs and rewards scale and learning.
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the fact. Sentence 5 ('The reason') explains it. Sentence 2 ('however') gives the risk. Sentence 4 gives the response. Sentence 1 questions its success. Order: 3-5-2-4-1.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. He replied that he had dropped them in the park, but the light was better here.
2. A man searching for his keys under a street lamp, the story goes, was asked where he had dropped them.
3. Researchers are prone to the same error when they study what is easy to measure and not what matters.
4. This is called the streetlight effect.
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 begins the story. Sentence 1 ('He replied') gives the punchline. Sentence 4 ('This') names the pattern. Sentence 3 ('the same error') applies it. Order: 2-1-4-3.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. It applies to things that do not age in the way living things do.
2. This is sometimes called the Lindy effect.
3. A book still read after a century is more likely to be read a century hence than one published last year.
4. The longer a book, a technology or an institution has survived, the longer it is likely to go on surviving.
5. The logic is that survival is itself evidence of robustness.
questions.explanation: Sentence 4 states the principle. Sentence 3 gives an example. Sentence 2 ('This') names it. Sentence 5 explains the logic. Sentence 1 ('It applies') states its scope. Order: 4-3-2-5-1.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. A free rider enjoys the benefit of a good without sharing the cost.
2. Governments therefore tax everyone to pay for such goods, instead of relying on voluntary contributions.
3. If everyone reasons in this way, the good is not provided.
4. Clean air and national defence are classic examples of goods that invite free riding.
questions.explanation: Sentence 1 defines the free rider. Sentence 3 ('If everyone reasons in this way') gives the consequence. Sentence 4 gives examples. Sentence 2 ('therefore') gives the remedy. Order: 1-3-4-2.
